newsitem.title: JAPAN: Cloudy skies seen ahead for Japanese airlines.
newsitem.headline: Cloudy skies seen ahead for Japanese airlines.

text.p: High fuel prices that have hurt Japanese airlines are easing, but they still face cloudy skies ahead and need to cut costs significantly to cope with an ever-more competitive environment, analysts say.

Japan's top two carriers -- Japan Airlines Co Ltd (JAL) and All Nippon Airways Co Ltd (ANA) -- are both expected to announce lower operating profits for the year that ended on March 31, 1997, due to higher oil prices and a weak yen.
Analysts forecast JAL would post nil profit at the operating level and second-ranked ANA would suffer a 30-percent profit drop.
They said the two firms, which will announce their earnings results at the end of this week, still face a bumpy ride.
"Oil prices rose 30 to 40 percent last fiscal year...This makes the airlines' costs about 60 to 70 percent higher than those of American carriers," said Naoko Matsumoto of Merrill Lynch Japan Inc.
"Japanese airlines are rationalising their operations, but they have to come up with a way to cut costs to the level of U.S. airlines," she said.
Average ticket prices to and from Japan dropped considerably in 1996/97, due to oversupply caused by a rise in capacity at Kansai International Airport, which opened in Osaka, western Japan, in 1994.
Analysts said the lower fares, despite elevated costs, made it difficult for Japanese carriers to increase profits, and a weak yen lowered the number of Japanese travelling abroad.

A worrying blip on the radar screen is a U.S. proposal for an "open-skies" agreement -- the lifting of all regulations for all carriers. Japan fears this suggestion, put forward in bilateral airline talks, would lead to monopolistic alliances advantageous to U.S. carriers.
Given such a tough environment, Matsumoto said JAL was likely to post a nil parent operating profit for 1996/97 after an actual 15.4 billion yen ($132 million) profit in 1995/96.
JAL would have to cut costs drastically to improve its business, although lower fuel costs should ameliorate the situation for the current year started in April, she said.

In March, JAL forecast a parent current loss of 20 billion yen ($172 million) for last fiscal year, down from an earlier forecast of nil profit. Current profit is pre-tax and includes gains and losses from investments.

ANA, Japan's number-one domestic carrier, is expected to have a 30 percent fall in its operating profit for 1996/97 as its sales tumbled even though it lowered prices for domestic flights, said Jun Harada, an analyst at Yamaichi Research Institute of Securities and Economics.
Harada forecast that ANA would manage a parent operating profit of 19 billion yen ($163 million), compared with an actual 27.3 billion yen ($235 million) in fiscal 1995/96.
ANA said in October it would post a parent current profit of 17.5 billion yen ($150 million) for 1996/97, but did not give any estimate for operating profit.
ANA has not been helped by management wrangling.

It said last week that honorary chairman Tokuji Wakasa would resign as a director, a move media reports said would be to take responsibility for a dispute which prompted the resignation of Seiji Fukatsu as president.
Wakasa, an 82-year-old former vice transport minister, has been under fire since ANA announced Fukatsu would resign after a board of directors meeting in late June.
Japanese media reports said Fukatsu made his abrupt decision due to disagreements with Wakasa over management and personnel issues, including a plan to restructure the airline.
Despite its problems, analysts say Japan's airline industry, long criticised for being protected by hefty regulations, is slowly moving towards a freer operating environment

This was shown by the launch last year of two new domestic carriers, the first new domestic airlines in more than 40 years. The more prominent new-born, Skymark Airlines Co Ltd, was formed last November by discount ticket agency H.I.S Co Ltd.
However, analysts said it would be premature to assume the new carriers would pose an immediate threat to established airlines.
